lessons.title: Your first Rust program
lessons.passage: A program is a set of instructions for a computer. The text you edit is its source code; main.rs is the Rust source filename shown here. This program has one instruction: display the message Hello, Rust! You do not need any previous programming experience for this lesson. The first line, fn main() {, marks where the program begins. fn means “function”, a named group of instructions; main is the name Rust starts with. The empty parentheses mean main takes no inputs here. The opening { and closing } enclose its instructions. Keep these outer lines as they are for now. The middle line, println!("Hello, Rust!");, displays the text between the double quotes. Write println! including its exclamation mark: it is Rust’s supplied print command. Its parentheses hold the message, and the semicolon ends the instruction. The quotes mark text in the source; they are not printed. A compiler checks your source and translates it into a program the browser can run. Your first run downloads about 58 MB of compiler files. Later runs in the same tab reuse the prepared compiler.

lessons.title: Run instructions in order
lessons.passage: Rust follows the instructions in main from top to bottom. Two println! instructions produce two separate lines in that same order. A newline means moving to the next output line. println! adds one after its message, so you do not need to put a line break inside the quotes. Use a new source line and a semicolon for each instruction. Indentation—the spaces before each instruction—helps you see what is inside main.

lessons.title: Give values names
lessons.passage: A value is a piece of data, such as text or a number. let gives a value a name. In let message = "Hello, Rust!";, message is the name and the quoted greeting is its value. The = sign here means “bind this name to this value”. The semicolon ends the instruction, just as it ends a print instruction. To display the value, write println!("{message}");. The braces inside these quotes are a placeholder: Rust replaces {message} with the value named message. These are different from the outer braces that enclose main. An equivalent spelling is println!("{}", message);. An empty placeholder takes the value supplied after the comma. Later examples use this form to display a calculation or function result directly. This program needs only main, let, and println!. Functions that return values and borrowed text types come in later lessons.

lessons.title: Change a value with mut
lessons.passage: A whole number is another kind of value. Write let score = 10; without quotes to store the number ten. With quotes, "10" would be text instead. A binding declared with let normally keeps its original value. To permit changes, add mut: let mut score = 10;. mut is short for mutable, meaning changeable. After that declaration, score = 15; replaces the stored number. score += 5; is a shorter way to say score = score + 5;. The + sign adds numbers. Only mark a binding mut when the program needs to change it. The worked program starts at 10 and adds 5 twice.

lessons.title: Say what kind of number you mean
lessons.passage: A type describes what kind of value a name can hold. Rust often infers, or works out, the type. A colon lets you state it: let score: u32 = 90;. u32 means an unsigned 32-bit whole number. A bit is a storage position that holds 0 or 1; using more bits allows more possible values. Unsigned means zero or positive, never negative. u32 holds values from 0 through 4,294,967,295. You do not need to memorise this limit. u8 is a smaller whole number from 0 through 255; it will represent small storage units called bytes later. u64 allows larger whole numbers. usize is Rust’s whole-number type for collection lengths and positions. Each name identifies a numeric type, not a variable. Here all arithmetic uses small u32 values. A value must fit its type: a negative value cannot be stored in u32.

lessons.passage: Before running, the compiler checks whether your source follows Rust’s rules. If it finds a problem, this lesson shows Compiler messages below the same code. lessons.title: Check a result with an assertion
lessons.passage: An assertion is a check written in the program. assert_eq!(actual, expected); continues only when both values are equal. It prints nothing when the check passes. lessons.title: Own a piece of editable text
lessons.passage: The quoted text you have printed is written directly into the program. A String is a value that owns editable text. lessons.title: Distinguish bytes from letters
lessons.passage: A byte is a small storage unit represented by u8, a number from zero through 255. UTF-8 is the rule Rust uses to represent text as bytes. English letters such as A occupy one byte, but é occupies two. text.len() counts bytes, not visible letters. café has five bytes: c, a, and f use one each, and é uses two. This distinction matters when a file reserves a fixed number of bytes for a name. Double quotes describe text such as "Ada". Single quotes describe one Rust character, such as 'A'. A character has type char. To put a quote inside a character literal, escape it as '\''; \n inside text represents a newline and \0 represents a zero byte. Text provides .bytes() to visit its UTF-8 bytes and .chars() to visit its characters. A for loop can visit them as it visits a numeric range. A later lesson will explain the iterator interface behind these operations.

lessons.passage: A recursive function calls itself on a smaller problem. factorial(0) is 1; factorial(n) for positive n is n multiplied by factorial(n−1). The base case ends the chain of calls. lessons.title: Linked lists and owned links
lessons.passage: A singly linked list stores a value and a link to the next node. Option> is either an owned successor or None at the tail. Box owns a heap-allocated value and has a known pointer-sized representation, allowing a recursive Node type to have finite size. Box::new creates the allocation. lessons.title: Binary search trees and height
lessons.passage: A binary search tree keeps smaller keys in the left subtree and larger keys in the right. Each child is an Option>, reusing the owned-link representation from linked lists. lessons.title: Split, merge, and preserve invariants
lessons.passage: TinyDB deliberately uses small capacities: four rows per leaf and five child pointers per branch. Occupancy means how many entries a node currently holds. These small limits let a short lab reveal structural changes. The helper is called on a known, nonempty overflow vector. For five sorted keys, split_off(len / 2) leaves two on the left and returns three on the right. The first right key becomes the parent separator, but remains a data key in the right leaf. In the full tree, the new right leaf is linked into the leaf chain and inserted into its parent. An overflowing parent splits too; a split root creates a new level. Deletion needs the opposite repair: borrow an entry from a sibling with spare capacity, or merge two small nodes and free the removed page. A one-child root collapses. These are the full implementation’s invariants; .check validates them after the lab operations.

lessons.title: Find your way around the complete source
lessons.passage: The complete TinyDB program is longer than a lesson example. Row validates one record. Database owns the page arena and index operations. Session chooses staged or committed state and saves files. Start from the named operation you are studying, not from the first import in the file. Private helpers such as node, alloc, and branch are supplied operations. Read their input and output types, then their comments. The eight optional implementation projects remove one operation at a time while keeping the other helpers available. You are not expected to reconstruct the entire program unaided. Path is a borrowed filesystem path and PathBuf is an owned path, analogous to borrowed text and an owned String. The standard Read, BufRead, and Write traits supply input/output methods. Trait imports make those methods available; these are standard-library APIs, not new SQL rules. #[cfg(...)] is a conditional-compilation attribute: it includes a section only for a named build target. The reference uses it for native file syncing versus the browser’s virtual filesystem. Those platform-specific helpers are provided scaffold; do not edit them for a tree or parser project. All later transaction and recovery lessons still use small, complete Rust programs first. The full source and project starters are an optional extension after the relevant lessons, rather than a prerequisite for following the core course. Some supplied code uses impl FnOnce(...) for a closure called at most once, or collect::>>() to gather successful iterator items while propagating the first error. The underscore asks Rust to infer the element type. These combine the closure, trait-bound, Result, and collection ideas already taught. Named enum-variant fields can be bound or renamed in a match, such as rows: mut target; the pattern borrows or moves the declared fields according to the same ownership rules.

lessons.title: Stage changes before publishing
lessons.passage: A transaction groups changes into one publish decision. Committed state is the last accepted version. Staged state is a candidate version that may still be committed or discarded. TinyDB begins by cloning its current database. The small helper below uses .to_vec() to make an owned copy of a borrowed slice, then changes only that copy. BEGIN starts the candidate, and reads in the same session see its staged changes. The next lessons show rollback and commit. This bounded design copies state for clarity rather than providing concurrent database sessions. Each browser Run starts a fresh process. BEGIN and its COMMIT or ROLLBACK must therefore appear in the same script; an open transaction rolls back when that input ends.

lessons.title: Rollback discards the candidate
lessons.passage: ROLLBACK abandons all staged changes in this transaction. It does not delete rows that were committed before BEGIN. Option> makes this state explicit: Some(candidate) means a transaction has a staged vector, and None means no active candidate. Assigning None drops that owned candidate. .is_none() is a boolean check for the None variant. The test verifies both that staged state disappears and that the committed vector remains unchanged. TinyDB leaves a transaction active after a statement error, preserving the previous staged state. The learner then chooses whether to inspect, commit, or roll back.

lessons.title: Commit one new generation
lessons.passage: COMMIT publishes a valid candidate as the next committed state. A generation is a counter identifying that published database version; it is not a row count. Two successful changes inside one transaction produce one new generation. A standalone write autocommits through the same commit operation, producing its own increment. checked_add prevents the counter from wrapping and making a new state look like an old version. The full commit protocol records intent before installing pages; the next chapter explains that journal. A database generation and a browser workspace revision count different things. The final persistence lesson distinguishes the Rust database commit from saving a browser file snapshot.

lessons.title: Record intent before installing pages
lessons.passage: A journal records the intended change before replacing committed pages. TinyDB’s RWL2 journal contains a full after-image: the complete candidate RDB2 snapshot for the next generation. The ordered steps are: write a prepared journal, write its committed marker, install the main snapshot, then remove the journal. A prepared marker alone does not commit the candidate. A committed marker says recovery should redo the saved after-image. .crash prepare, .crash commit, and .crash install deliberately interrupt the next commit at those stages. Reopen the database in a second Run to observe the actual recovery decision. These commands are teaching simulations. Native file syncing asks the operating system to flush writes, while a browser virtual filesystem has no physical fsync guarantee. The webpage saves a snapshot after the simulated exit; an actual tab kill has a different persistence boundary, covered in the final lesson. Recovery happens automatically when the database file is reopened. The .recover inspection command reports the completed recovery generation; it is not required to trigger replay.

lessons.title: Replay once, verify on repetition
lessons.passage: Idempotent means repeating an operation has the same effect as doing it once. Recovery needs this property because an interruption may happen after pages are installed but before journal cleanup. A committed journal targeting generation N can install over its base generation N−1. If N is already installed, the exact snapshot bytes must match before removing the journal. Matching generation numbers alone do not prove matching data. A different generation or different bytes are a conflict: report the error and retain the files rather than guessing which state to keep. Checksums detect accidental byte changes, while structural validation checks the tree rules. Neither check authenticates a file against deliberate rewriting.

lessons.title: Save files without overwriting another tab
lessons.passage: A process is one running copy of a program. When it finishes normally, it returns an exit code: zero for success or a nonzero number for an error. A runtime trap means execution could not continue normally, such as a failed assertion in this browser build. The Rust program runs with a private virtual filesystem: an in-memory set of filenames and bytes supplied for this Run. A normal exit returns its complete file set to the webpage. The webpage stores that set in IndexedDB, a browser-provided local database separate from TinyDB itself. A workspace revision counts successful whole-file-set saves, including reads that create or recover files. It is separate from TinyDB’s committed generation. Saving compares the expected revision with the current revision inside one atomic browser storage transaction: either the complete new set is saved, or none of that save is published. A stale tab keeps its unsaved candidate downloadable rather than overwriting another tab. An ordinary nonzero process exit can include earlier successful commits. Stop, traps, or timeouts return no candidate snapshot and keep the previous saved files. Browser storage can be denied or evicted, so download important files. This explains the recovery lab boundary: a deliberate .crash exit can save the journal plus main file together, while an actual tab termination during the Run leaves the prior IndexedDB snapshot. No JavaScript or operating-system knowledge is required to use these rules.
